_readme: Content for page IV. Edit text here, not in iv.js. Every evidence item needs sourceIds that exist in 'sources'. Ratings are team judgments (1-5, higher = more promising; for risk, higher = lower risk). Pitch-length edit: about 2-3 evidence items per slide; numbers shown in a chart are not repeated in text. Open checks before presenting: confirm Stanford SNT's regulatory status; company revenue figures stay hidden until verified against filings; confirm the timeline dates listed in charts.stimulationTimeline.dateNotes.

demo.heading: Timing TMS to the brain's own rhythm

lede.text: The motor cortex hums at about ten beats a second, a wave called the mu rhythm. Magnetic pulses that land on the wave's trough have produced stronger effects than pulses at random times.

But no one can see where a wave is until it has passed, and every system takes time to fire. So we trained a small neural network to predict the wave ahead of time. Here it runs against the standard method on recorded EEG from a person it never trained on.

notes.text: Across 9 people it never trained on, it put 71% of pulses on target at a 40 ms delay, versus 53% for the standard method and 25% for untimed TMS.
This is recorded EEG, not live stimulation, and whether mu phase changes TMS effects is still debated.

thesis.headline: Brain stimulation has the most promise, and the other two fields will reach patients through it.

sentences.text: Stimulation is the only one of the three already improving patient outcomes, with independent randomized trials and an adaptive system approved in 2025.
Connectomics will tell stimulation where to aim; biohybrid implants may one day replace the electrode that delivers it.
The bottleneck is the last mile (patient selection, programming, referral, payment), and that is where new companies can win.

framework.intro: Six criteria, each borrowed from a tool that funders, regulators, or investors already use to judge medical technology.

criteria.name: Magnitude of the problem and potential impact
questions: How big is the problem, and how much better could this be?
criteria.lookedFor: Disease burden; limits of current care.

criteria.name: Scientific evidence and technical maturity
questions: Does it reliably work, ideally in humans?

criteria.name: Translation and time to impact
questions: What blocks real use, and for how long?

criteria.name: Customer demand and adoption
questions: Who needs it, who pays, and why switch?

criteria.name: Commercial viability and scalability
criteria.test: Can this become a sustainable business?
questions: Can it become a scalable business?

criteria.name: Risk, uncertainty, and responsible deployment
questions: What could break the thesis or harm people?

ratingScale.direction: Higher is always better. For risk (C6), higher means lower risk.
ratingScale.note: Ratings are team judgments, not measurements.

biodesignNote.text: Following Stanford Biodesign's guidance, we rated only what is known today.

framework.lensSummary: Equal counts every criterion the same, Patients puts benefit, proof, speed and safety first, Founders puts demand and business viability first, and Science puts impact on understanding and the quality of the evidence first.

c2.rationale: Fly maps predict; mammal maps are tiny samples.

c3.rationale: Whole mouse brain 10 to 15 years out.

c1.rationale: Large, growing needs; beats drugs in trials.

c2.rationale: Multiple independent randomized trials, some blinded.

c3.rationale: In clinic now; programming still hard.

c4.rationale: Clear benefit, but few patients referred.

c6.rationale: Surgical risk, failed sham trials, unequal access.

fields.name: Human brain stimulation
fields.verdict: Already helping patients; the frontier is personalization and access.
fields.definition: Electrical or magnetic energy that changes brain activity: deep brain stimulation (DBS) through implanted electrodes, or transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) through a coil on the head. Adaptive DBS adjusts itself in real time.

slides.verdict: Large, growing needs, and stimulation already outperforms drugs.

evidence.text: Parkinson's cases may more than double by 2050, to 25.2 million.
In the EARLYSTIM trial, quality of life rose 26% with stimulation and fell 1% on drugs alone.
Stanford's 5-day SNT protocol beat sham for depression (50% versus 20.8% remission), though remission faded over 12 weeks.

slides.verdict: The most mature field by far, with one cautionary tale.

evidence.text: Randomized trials favored DBS over best medical therapy; in the VA trial, good 'on' time rose from 6.4 to 10.9 hours a day.

evidence.qualifier: Many trials at high risk of bias
evidence.text: A 2026 meta-analysis of 30 randomized comparisons found robust, high-certainty antidepressant effects for TMS.

slides.verdict: In clinic now; what remains is precision and programming.

evidence.text: Adaptive DBS programming is incompletely defined; in one clinic, only 9 of 20 patients offered it qualified.
UCSF is testing an automated pipeline to recommend adaptive DBS settings for non-specialist clinics.

caveats: Psychiatric DBS timelines hinge on the TRANSCEND trial.

slides.verdict: Patients who get it stay on it, but most never get it.

evidence.text: 98% of ADAPT-PD participants chose to remain on adaptive DBS.
Only about 10% of eligible Parkinson's patients are referred; many clinicians don't realize how safe DBS is.

caveats: Adoption data are mostly from Parkinson's.

slides.verdict: A reimbursed market exists; the opening is software for personalized programming.

evidence.text: Most insurers cover DBS for Parkinson's, and adaptive DBS runs on sensing devices already in use.
DBS needs skilled clinicians to program it, and the devices now record data that could help automate it.

We built a piece of that software: a small neural network that predicts the brain's mu rhythm from scalp EEG, so a TMS pulse lands on the wave's trough, the timing linked to stronger effects. Try it at the top of this page.

Tested on 9 people it never trained on, it put 71% of simulated pulses on target at a 40 ms system delay, versus 53% for the standard method and 25% for untimed TMS. It beat both published methods for all 9 people.
At a 60 ms delay it was as accurate as the standard method with no delay, so cheaper hardware could deliver timed TMS. A few minutes of each person's own EEG made it better for all 9.
One study found no effect of mu phase on how strongly TMS excites the motor cortex, so the benefit of timing still has to be shown in patients.

caveats: The software opening is our inference.
Our demo used recorded EEG, not live stimulation.

slides.verdict: Surgery carries real risk, and access is unequal.

evidence.text: In the VA trial, 49 DBS patients had serious adverse events versus 15 on medication, including one death.
Women and racial and ethnic minorities are less likely to receive DBS, even at equal severity.

caveats: Most safety data come from experienced centers.

fields.name: Connectomics
fields.verdict: Complete in a fly, a cubic millimeter in us.
fields.definition: Maps of how neurons connect, from every synapse in tiny tissue samples to MRI maps of major fiber tracts. A research tool: it helps patients only through what is built on it.

overviewReadiness.label: Whole maps of small brains (worm, fly)

slides.verdict: Maybe the biggest problem of the three, but it helps patients only indirectly.

evidence.text: Nervous-system conditions were the top cause of lost healthy life in 2021, affecting about 3.4 billion people.
A simulation built only from fly wiring correctly predicted which neurons sense taste and start feeding.

slides.verdict: Fly maps replicate and predict; mammal maps are tiny, partly checked samples.

evidence.text: Two independent fly maps agreed on most cell types and strong connections, but about a third of earlier proposed types could not be re-identified.
Tracing about 1,500 mouse neurons took years and over a million manual fixes.

readiness.label: Whole maps of small brains (worm, fly)

slides.verdict: Whole mouse brain: 10 to 15 years out. Whole human brain: we found no credible timeline.

evidence.text: Wellcome's experts set a whole mouse connectome as a 10 to 15 year goal; proofreading alone might take about 100,000 person-years today.
E11 Bio's protein barcodes let AI trace neurons on cheaper microscopes; it forecasts a mouse map in about five years.

slides.verdict: Buyers are researchers and funders; clinical demand arrives through stimulation.

evidence.text: NIH's BRAIN CONNECTS program is building pipelines to map whole mammalian brains.
Demand grows as maps get cheaper; E11 Bio claims a path to 100 times lower cost.

caveats: Desk research only; no buyer interviews yet.

slides.verdict: Weak as a business by design: the data is free and open.

evidence.text: Flagship datasets (MICrONS, FlyWire, E11 Bio) are released free and open.
Only a few centers could image a whole mouse brain, but later software stages could be widely distributed.

slides.verdict: Little direct patient risk, but noisy maps can mislead.

evidence.text: MRI tractography produces more invalid fiber bundles than valid ones, a danger if maps guide treatment.
Wiring maps leave out neuromodulators, which reshape how circuits behave.

caveats: Low direct risk is our judgment; mapping uses tissue outside the body.

fields.name: Biohybrid implants
fields.verdict: Proven in the arm, promised in the brain.
fields.definition: Electronics paired with living cells, so tissue meets biology instead of bare metal: a muscle graft amplifying a cut nerve in the arm, or engineered neurons wiring into the brain.

slides.verdict: The biggest claimed upside, but the brain benefits are projections.

evidence.text: Nearly 5.4 million Americans live with paralysis and nearly 2 million with limb loss.
Science Corp claims orders of magnitude more bandwidth; an outside expert says its device isn't yet an interface on its own.

slides.verdict: Proven in the arm; in the brain, a one-way rodent proof of concept.

evidence.text: A 2026 meta-analysis (238 patients) found no neuromas after RPNI surgery versus 20 of 99 with standard care.
In mice, Science Corp's grafted neurons integrated, but behavior change wasn't statistically significant and signals flowed one way.

readiness.label: RPNI for pain prevention (biological only, no electronics)
RPNI with implanted electrodes for prosthetic control

caveats: An RPNI alone is purely biological; it becomes biohybrid with electrodes.

slides.verdict: A human brain device is likely a decade or more away.

evidence.text: Developers need a universal, immune-cloaked cell line; patient-specific grafts would cost over $1 million each.
No two-way biohybrid interface has been shown, and Science Corp's first human device is a cell-free sensor.

slides.verdict: Real need, but demand for a brain biohybrid is untested.

evidence.text: Many adults abandon prostheses: average rejection rates were 26% (body-powered) and 23% (electric).
Investors are paying for now: Science Corp raised a $230 million Series C at a reported $1.5 billion valuation.

caveats: No patient interviews yet; funding signals belief, not demand.

slides.verdict: Cost, regulation, and slow payment make the business speculative today.

evidence.text: No company has mapped the regulatory path for a device containing living neurons.
Small device makers had a 19.4% five-year chance of Medicare coverage, versus 67.9% for large ones.
Science Corp is hedging by selling electronics and tooling to other BCI companies.

slides.verdict: Living, gene-modified cells add new unknowns to normal implant risks.

evidence.text: The graft must evade the immune system, and the long-term design uses light-sensitive, gene-modified neurons.
Neural-data privacy law is new: Colorado and California passed the first state laws in 2024.

explanation.text: Connectivity maps already predict which DBS placements help, and they aim Stanford's SNT.
Closed-loop devices stimulate only on a symptom's brain signature, so better decoding means better timing.
Our demo shows the timing gain: predicting the motor rhythm 40 ms ahead put 71% of simulated TMS pulses on target, versus 53% with the standard method.
Biohybrids aim to reach more neurons with less damage, but are still in animals.

alsoAnswers.heading: What this says about Questions 1 and 2

items.title: Scale versus modality
items.body: Both bets are rational, on different clocks. Scaling metal electrodes (Neuralink) builds on real human use but fights scarring that degrades signals. Living-neuron interfaces (Science Corp) could sidestep that limit but have no human data yet.

items.title: What holds neurotech back
items.body: Three gates beyond the science: beating sham, getting paid (a median 5.7-year Medicare wait, longer for small firms), and getting referred (about 10% of eligible Parkinson's patients). Optogenetics has reached just one patient, in the eye. If regulation changes, our evidence points first to payment, which CMS's proposed RAPID pathway targets.

connectomeScale.title: How much brain has been mapped
connectomeScale.summary: Worm and fly brains are fully mapped; mammalian maps are cubic-millimeter samples; whole mouse and human brains are unmapped.
connectomeScale.takeaway: Complete in a fly, a cubic millimeter in us.
connectomeScale.countNote: Counts as reported; some studies count all cells, some neurons only.

points.label: Whole mouse brain
points.scope: About 1,000 times the data of the human sample

annotation.text: A whole mouse brain needs about 1,000 times the data of the 1.4-petabyte human sample.

connectomeScale.renderingNote: The whole mouse point has no reported neuron count in our sources; render it as a hollow dashed marker positioned between the human sample and whole human brain with the label only, and do not invent a number.

biohybridEvidence.title: Where biohybrid evidence stands
biohybridEvidence.summary: In human surgery for pain prevention; small human studies for prosthetic control; animal-only in the brain.
biohybridEvidence.takeaway: Proven in the arm, promised in the brain.

steps.label: Brain biohybrid in humans
steps.detail: Not yet attempted; first human device will be a sensor without cells.

steps.label: RPNI with electrodes for prosthetic control

stimulationTimeline.title: Two evidence tracks in brain stimulation
stimulationTimeline.summary: Parkinson's DBS: positive trials 2006 to 2020, adaptive DBS approved 2025. Depression: two DBS trials stopped, SNT positive 2022, TRANSCEND begun 2025.
stimulationTimeline.dateNotes: RECLAIM's report year (2015) comes from the Cleveland Clinic summary of its Biological Psychiatry publication; BROADEN's publication year (2017) comes from Medscape. Verify exact dates if the team wants month-level precision. INTREPID is placed at 2020, the year of the Lancet Neurology exchange about its results; confirm the primary publication year.

coverageGap.title: FDA approval is not the finish line
coverageGap.summary: 44% of 64 novel FDA-authorized devices reached any Medicare coverage, after a median 5.7 years; small makers fared far worse.

bars.label: Novel devices reaching any Medicare coverage

headlineStat.text: Median wait: 5.7 years after FDA authorization.
